# Blower Motor Location on my Wrangler

If you are troubleshooting the A/C system on a Jeep Wrangler TJ, specifically models from around 1999, finding the blower motor can feel like searching for a needle in a haystack. Online forums often suggest the unit is tucked underneath the glove box. While this advice isn't entirely wrong, it represents only half of the story and can lead to unnecessary frustration if you assume that's the sole location.

In many 1999 Wrangler TJs, the primary blower motor is indeed mounted directly under the dashboard, accessible by removing the lower panel beneath the glove compartment. However, digging through that area often yields nothing because the specific component might be further integrated into the HVAC housing or obscured by electrical harnesses and insulation. The images provided in typical community discussions show this exact scenario: you remove the trim, expose the cavity, and find only wiring or empty space where a massive motor should be sitting. This isn't a mistake on your part; it is a common point of confusion due to the vehicle's compact engine bay and the specific routing of the HVAC ducting in these models.

To approach this systematically, you need to understand the physical layout rather than just following a visual guide. The blower motor assembly is typically mounted on a bracket that sits against the firewall or the inner fender well, depending on the exact trim level and aftermarket modifications. If your A/C compressor has been removed or the system is non-functional, it is highly probable that the blower motor itself has also failed or been unplugged during previous repairs.

When inspecting the area under the glove box, look beyond the immediate cavity. You often need to trace the large-diameter ductwork that runs from the heater core area toward the firewall. The motor is frequently attached to a housing that extends further back than initially visible. In some configurations, the motor is located behind a secondary panel that requires additional fasteners to be removed before the unit can be accessed. If you are seeing only wires and no mechanical component, check for a blown fuse or a disconnected connector first. A lack of power will make the motor appear "missing" even if it is physically present.

There is also the possibility of a secondary blower motor setup in certain configurations, though less common on stock TJs. Some enthusiasts have upgraded to dual-speed setups where a smaller auxiliary blower might be mounted in a different location, but for standard replacement, you are looking for the main unit driving the cabin airflow. The challenge lies in the fact that the HVAC box in these older vehicles is not easily accessible from a single entry point. You may need to remove the entire glove box assembly and slide it forward significantly to gain leverage on the retaining clips that hold the blower housing in place.

If you have cleared out all visible debris, inspected the ducting, and verified your electrical connections with a multimeter and still find no motor, it is likely that the unit has been removed entirely or was never installed correctly during a previous repair cycle. In this case, sourcing the correct replacement part number for the 1999 model year is critical, as cross-threading or using a motor from a different vehicle generation can cause alignment issues with the HVAC plenum.

For those documenting their repairs to help future technicians, taking detailed photographs of the wire harness connections before disconnecting them is essential. The connectors on these older Jeep models are notorious for being difficult to reseat without applying specific pressure angles. If you are unable to locate the motor despite extensive inspection under the dash and behind the firewall, consulting a service manual specific to the 1999 model year will provide the exact exploded view needed to identify hidden mounting points or secondary access panels that standard online advice overlooks.
